In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[category theory]], a '''quasi-abelian category''' is a [[pre-abelian category]] in which the [[pushout (category theory)|pushout]] of a [[kernel (category theory)|kernel]] along arbitrary morphisms is again a kernel and, dually, the [[pullback (category theory)|pullback]] of a [[cokernel (category theory)|cokernel]] along arbitrary morphisms is again a cokernel.

A quasi-abelian category is an [[exact category]].{{fact|date=July 2024}}

==Definition==

Let <math>\mathcal A</math> be a [[pre-abelian category]]. A morphism <math>f</math> is '''a kernel''' ('''a cokernel''') if there exists a morphism <math>g</math> such that <math>f</math> is a kernel (cokernel) of <math>g</math>. The category <math>\mathcal A</math> is '''quasi-abelian''' if for every kernel <math>f: X\rightarrow Y</math> and every morphism <math>h: X\rightarrow Z</math> in the pushout diagram

{{center|<math>
\begin{array}{ccc} 
X & \xrightarrow{f} & Y \\
\downarrow_{h} &  & \downarrow_{h'}\\
Z & \xrightarrow{f'} & Q
\end{array}
</math>}}

the morphism <math>f'</math> is again a kernel and, dually, for every cokernel <math>g: X\rightarrow Y</math> and every morphism <math>h: Z\rightarrow Y</math> in the pullback diagram

{{center|<math>
\begin{array}{ccc} 
P & \xrightarrow{g'} & Z \\
\downarrow_{h'} &  & \downarrow_{h}\\
X & \xrightarrow{g} & Y
\end{array}
</math>}}

the morphism <math>g'</math> is again a cokernel.

Equivalently, a quasi-abelian category is a pre-abelian category in which the system of all kernel-cokernel pairs forms an [[exact category|exact structure]].

Given a pre-abelian category, those kernels, which are stable under arbitrary pushouts, are sometimes called the '''semi-stable kernels'''. Dually, cokernels, which are stable under arbitrary pullbacks, are called '''semi-stable cokernels'''.<ref>Richman and Walker, 1977.</ref>

==Properties==

Let  <math>f</math> be a morphism in a quasi-abelian category. Then the induced morphism <math>\overline{f} : \operatorname{cok} \ker f \to \ker \operatorname{cok} f</math> is always a [[Morphism#Monomorphisms and epimorphisms|bimorphism]], i.e., a [[monomorphism]] and an [[epimorphism]]. A quasi-abelian category is therefore always [[semi-abelian category|semi-abelian]].

==Examples and non-examples ==

Every ''[[abelian category]]'' is quasi-abelian. Typical non-abelian examples arise in functional analysis.<ref>Prosmans, 2000.</ref>

* The category of [[Banach space]]s is quasi-abelian.
* The category of [[Fréchet space]]s is quasi-abelian.
* The category of ([[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]) [[locally convex space]]s is quasi-abelian.

Contrary to the claim by Beilinson,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Beilinson |first1=A |title=Remarks on topological algebras |journal=Moscow Mathematical Journal |date=2008 |volume=8 |issue=1}}</ref> the category of complete separated topological vector spaces with [[linear topology]] is not quasi-abelian.<ref name="exact">{{cite journal |last1=Positselski |first1=Leonid |title=Exact categories of topological vector spaces with linear topology |journal=Moscow Math. Journal |date=2024 |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=219–286}}</ref> On the other hand, the category of (arbitrary or Hausdorff) topological vector spaces with linear topology is quasi-abelian.<ref name="exact" />

==History==

The concept of quasi-abelian category was developed in the 1960s. The history is involved.<ref>Rump, 2008, p. 986f.</ref> This is in particular due to '''Raikov's conjecture''', which stated that the notion of a [[semi-abelian category]] is equivalent to that of a quasi-abelian category. Around 2005 it turned out that the conjecture is false.<ref>Rump, 2011, p. 44f.</ref>

==Left and right quasi-abelian categories==

By dividing the two conditions in the definition, one can define '''left quasi-abelian categories''' by requiring that cokernels are stable under pullbacks and '''right quasi-abelian categories''' by requiring that kernels stable under pushouts.<ref>Rump, 2001.</ref>
